newsitem.title: USA: CIA agent charged with selling secrets to Russia.
newsitem.headline: CIA agent charged with selling secrets to Russia.

text.p: The U.S. government on Monday said it arrested a CIA agent for selling secrets to Russia for at least two years, including compromising information about American spies about to be sent abroad.

The suspect, Harold Nicholson, a 16-year CIA veteran who had been chief of station in Romania and deputy chief in Malaysia, was charged with spying for Moscow since June 1994 in exchange for more than $100,000 in cash.
"He was not motivated by ideology but by greed," U.S. Attorney Helen Fahey told reporters in the Washington suburb of Alexandria, Virginia, where Nicholson was brought to court.
Nicholson was arrested on Saturday at Dulles Airport outside Washington as he was about to fly to Switzerland to meet his Russian handlers, the FBI said.
The CIA became suspicious after Nicholson appeared to be lying on two polygraph tests in October 1995. Investigators quickly focused on his travel and bank deposits.
Papers unsealed in court showed the divorced father of three earned about $73,000 a year but spent well beyond his means on travel, a girlfriend and his children.
The FBI found Nicholson, 46, had paid large bills in cash, opened a number of $1,000 joint accounts for his children and gave one child over $12,000 to help buy a car.
The FBI reviewed Nicholson's frequent-flyer records and found a pattern of travel abroad twice a year, followed by unexplained deposits and payments to his accounts,
The papers showed the FBI followed Nicholson around the world, tracking him to a meeting with Russian handlers at a taxi stand in Singapore last June.

The next day he made an $8,300 cash payment to his American Express account, flew to Bangkok where he picked up an unidentified female companion who lived there and took her to a resort in Hawaii. He paid his hotel bills in cash.
He has told the CIA he planned to marry her.

FBI officials intercepted postcards Nicholson mailed to his handlers, recovered classified information from his laptop computer, observed him photocopying secret documents and found classified data about Russia in his office that was unrelated to his CIA duties.

From 1994 until July 1996, Nicholson was an instructor at the CIA training centre in Virginia known as the "farm," where he trained agents in skills like recruiting foreigners to spy for the United States and avoiding spy-catchers.

Since July, Nicholson, who lives in a tan brick end-row townhouse in suburban Burke, Virginia, had served as a branch chief in the Counter-Terrorism Centre at the Central Intelligence Agency, where he outranked Ames Aldrich, another CIA employee who was caught selling secrets to Russia.

Nicholson had access to some of the most sensitive U.S. intelligence secrets, including reports from "access agents," foreign recruits who spy for the CIA often at great risk. As a staff instructor at the "farm" he had access to biographical information and the assignments of every new CIA officer trained there during his tenure, the CIA and FBI said.

At a joint news conference, Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Louis Freeh and CIA Director John Deutch said the case demonstrated a continuing threat to U.S. national security by foreign intelligence services.
Deutch said Nicholson appeared to have done far less damage than Ames, a confessed CIA turncoat arrested in 1994 after betraying dozens of agents and blowing many operations.

"We are not yet in a position to determine how many operations (Nicholson) may have compromised but it seems unlikely that the damage he caused in any way approaches that done by Ames," said Deutch. His CIA predecessor, James Woolsey, quit under fire for his handling of the Ames case.
Fahey, who is in overall charge of prosecuting the case, told reporters there was no evidence the Nicholson case was linked to Ames, who is now serving a life sentence.
Freeh said Nicholson had given Moscow the identities of "various CIA officers who were to be assigned to overseas posts," including Moscow.
Nicholson faced a possible death sentence if any secrets he sold led to deaths or involved highly classified military matters, but prosecutors said there was no such evidence yet.
Court papers alleged Nicholson had made $120,000 in unexplained bank deposits following personal trips abroad to London, New Delhi, Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur.
Dressed in a blue short-sleeve shirt and khaki pants, a bearded Nicholson was ordered held in custody pending a hearing next Monday.
